title: Reverse Proxies & API Gateways
summary: The reverse-proxy pattern underlying load balancers, CDNs, and API gateways alike, and how it differs from a forward proxy and a VPN.

slides.markdown:
A **reverse proxy** sits in front of one or more backend servers and handles requests on their behalf — clients only ever talk to the proxy, never directly to a backend. It's the pattern underneath load balancers, API gateways, and CDNs alike; understanding it once explains all three.

- Client → reverse proxy → backend. The client can't tell (or reach) the backend directly.
- Common jobs: TLS termination, caching, compression, and routing to the right backend.
- Different from a **forward proxy**, which sits in front of *clients*, not servers.

| | Forward proxy | Reverse proxy |
|---|---|---|
| Sits in front of | The client | The server(s) |
| Hides | The client's identity from the destination server | The backend server(s) from the client |
| Classic example | A corporate proxy filtering employee web access | Nginx in front of a web app |

A forward proxy answers "who is this request *from*, really?" for the server it reaches. A reverse proxy answers "who is actually serving this?" for the client making the request — the client only ever sees the proxy's address.

Putting a reverse proxy in front of your backends buys several things at once, cheaper than doing them in app code:

- **TLS termination** — the proxy decrypts HTTPS once; backends can speak plain HTTP internally.
- **Compression** — gzip/brotli applied centrally instead of in every backend.
- **Caching** — repeat responses served straight from the proxy, skipping the backend entirely.
- **Routing** — send different paths or hosts to different backend pools.

The theme: infrastructure-level concerns move out of application code and into one shared layer every request passes through.

![A client talking only to a reverse proxy, which forwards to one of several backend servers](assets/reverse-proxy-basic.svg)

The backend servers may not even have public IP addresses — the reverse proxy is the only thing clients can reach, which is also a security win: backends are unreachable directly from the internet.

assets.alt: A client talking only to a reverse proxy, which forwards to one of several backend servers

slides.markdown:
**TLS termination at the proxy** means HTTPS is decrypted once, at the proxy, and traffic to the backend runs as plain HTTP over a trusted internal network — simpler certificate management and less CPU spent on encryption per backend.

**End-to-end encryption** instead keeps traffic encrypted all the way to the backend. This matters when internal segments aren't fully trusted (shared cloud infra, compliance requirements) — see [tls-handshake-deep-dive](tls-handshake-deep-dive) for what's negotiated at each hop.

An **API gateway** is a reverse proxy specialized for API traffic, adding application-aware concerns on top of basic proxying:

- **Authentication** — validating an API key or JWT before a request ever reaches a backend.
- **Rate limiting** — capping requests per client/key to protect backends from abuse or overload.
- **Routing/aggregation** — sending `/users/*` to one microservice, `/orders/*` to another, sometimes combining multiple backend calls into one response.

It's the same reverse-proxy pattern, just with policy logic — auth, quotas, request shaping — layered on top.

| | Reverse proxy | Load balancer |
|---|---|---|
| Core job | Front a server (or servers), add features (TLS, caching, routing) | Distribute traffic across identical backends |
| Backend count | Can front a single server | Assumes a pool of interchangeable backends |
| Overlap | Fronting many backends *is* load balancing | Fronting HTTP *is* effectively a reverse proxy |

Most real deployments are one piece of software (Nginx, Envoy, HAProxy) doing both jobs at once.

slides.subTitle: Proxy vs VPN
slides.markdown: A common mix-up: **"a proxy is basically a VPN."** They solve different problems. A **reverse proxy** routes and terminates traffic for servers it's authorized to represent — no encryption of your entire network path is implied. A **VPN** creates an encrypted tunnel for a client's *own* traffic to reach a private network as if it were physically on it, changing *where* the client appears to be on the whole network, not just for one app's requests. Using one to explain the other in an interview is a fast way to signal you haven't drawn the distinction clearly.
